references.text: In Jesus' parable of the talents in [ref:Matt 25:24-25|Matthew 25:24-25], the lazy servant uses almost identical reasoning: he feared his master and described him as a harsh man who reaps where he did not sow and gathers where he did not scatter seed. This is the parallel passage to Luke's version of the parable.

In [ref:Luk 19:22|Luke 19:22], the master responds by judging the servant based on his own words – if he knew the master was harsh, he should at least have put the money in the bank. The master's response shows that the servant's fear was not a valid excuse.
[ref:Ordsp 26:13|Proverbs 26:13] describes the lazy person who finds excuses to avoid action, just as this servant uses fear as an excuse to do nothing with his mina.
[ref:Ordsp 22:13|Proverbs 22:13] speaks of the lazy person who makes excuses ('there is a lion outside!'), a parallel to the servant's excuse of fear used to justify his passivity.

[ref:Rom 8:15|Romans 8:15] contrasts the spirit of slavery that leads to fear with the Spirit of adoption. The servant's slavish fear of the master in Luke 19:21 stands in contrast to a true relationship with God characterized by trust.

[ref:1 Joh 4:18|1 John 4:18] says that perfect love drives out fear. The servant's fear-based relationship with the master reveals a distorted image of God that paralyzes into passivity instead of motivating service.
In [ref:Matt 25:26|Matthew 25:26], the master calls the servant 'wicked and lazy,' revealing that the real reason behind the fear was laziness and disobedience, not genuine reverence for the master.
